1:
The verb of forbearing is a vivid one and each of them reaches for a different picture of it. Robertson derives it from the word for a roof and gives its range as covering, concealing, keeping off and enduring, a sense he finds in the papyri too. Ellicott hears in it a vessel over-full and bursting with what it holds. Gill makes the suppressed longing a fire in the bones, held in with pain until, like the prophet weary with forbearing, they could stay no longer, or else a burden borne up under as long as strength lasted. Who is meant by the plural is less easily settled, and the four who take it up divide. Ellicott argues for the writer alone, on the strength of the limitation two chapters earlier and of the outright singular three verses later. Robertson allows the literary plural but thinks two men more likely. Wesley names the second of them. Gill widens it further, to the three who had worked in the city together. Clarke leaves the persons aside for the motive: no report could be had without a messenger express, and the writer preferred sending one to remaining in uncertainty.

Being left at Athens raises a difficulty with the history, since Acts has the two companions rejoining the writer at Corinth and never places them in Athens at all. Ellicott concedes the difficulty is not a light one, then argues from the tense that the phrase absolutely requires an act of parting with somebody, so it cannot mean merely enduring loneliness a while longer; he concludes they must have joined him at Athens and been sent back almost at once, one into Macedonia and one to Thessalonica, and explains the silence of Acts about the first by saying it held no interest for this letter's readers. Barnes reaches the same conclusion by a different road, listing three circumstances that make an Athenian visit probable: a message was sent back for them to come at once, the stay in the city was made on purpose to wait for them, and the departure was unhurried, since he saw the place, disputed daily and made converts before going on. Robertson simply states the sequence as though it were settled, both arriving, one sent straight back, the other despatched later.

Calvin puts the weight on the word alone and treats the sending as a costly proof. Timothy was the most faithful companion he had and at that moment the only one, so that doing without him was distressing; that he chose to be left by himself rather than leave them deserted is the token of affection the passage turns on, and it also lends authority to the teaching they had received from the man he sent. The titles given to Timothy occupy the rest. Ellicott reports that most of the best editors judge the received text here interpolated and would read "our brother, and God's fellow-worker in the gospel," and asks why so familiar a figure should be particularised unless he carried the letter and was to be paid deference despite his youth; Robertson notes the same variant and adds that the word for minister is used here in its general sense and not of the office of deacon. Clarke recalls that Timothy was a youth at his conversion and is elsewhere called a son, and turns the title into a rebuke: preaching was God's work and there were no sinecures then. Henry makes the same point: the man was junior in age, inferior in gifts and of lower rank, an evangelist under an apostle, and is still called brother, which he takes for humility and a wish to raise him in the churches' esteem. Gill grounds the word in a shared household rather than an office, and Henry adds that ministers should strengthen one another's hands rather than contend.
3:
The verb translated "moved" is a strange one and the commentators trace it through the same chain to different ends. Barnes reports that it occurs nowhere else in the New Testament and means properly to wag, as dogs wag their tails in fondness, then to caress or fawn or flatter, and only then to waver from dread; he settles on being so agitated by the terror of persecution as to forsake one's religion. Ellicott follows the identical route and prefers "seduced," describing the animal fawning on its master, then the wheedling that detaches a man from his resolution by insinuating representations, whether of flattery or, as here, of fear. Robertson keeps the beguiling sense as the one that suits, and points out that the familiar rendering rests on a different reading found in two manuscripts and in the papyri. Clarke reduces it to apostasy from Christianity. On whose sufferings are in view the two who address it disagree flatly: Ellicott corrects the preposition, holding that the afflictions meant are chiefly the readers' own and not the writer's, while Gill takes them for the writer's, endured in preaching among them and feared to be what might shake young converts.

Being appointed to affliction divides them harder still. Calvin takes it as the terms of the calling, so that believers have no reason to be dismayed at persecution as though it were new or unusual, this being the condition on which men are Christians at all; and since they had been forewarned they were bound to fight the more bravely. Ellicott extends the pronoun to all Christian people and makes election into the church an election to suffering, summing it in four words, no cross, no crown. Clarke refuses the whole construction. God appoints nothing of this kind but permits it, he says, having made man a free agent; what the words mean is only that we lie open to such things and they are unavoidable as the world now stands. Barnes declines to fix the reference at all, allowing that the pronoun may mean the writer, or the writer with his readers, or Christians at large, and observing that the general sense serves best, since it shows the readers had received only the common lot. Robertson states it as a duty rather than a doctrine: Christians are set there to be beguiled by tribulations, and must resist.

Chrysostom stops at the sending itself and asks the question nobody else raises. How is it that a man who had heard unutterable words and been caught up to the third heaven did not know how matters stood at Thessalonica, when the distance was not great and the parting had been short? His answer is that the saints did not know all things, and he supports it from three cases: Elisha, who did not know what ailed the woman; Elijah, who said he only was left and was told of seven thousand; and Samuel, sent to anoint and warned not to look on the countenance or the height of the stature. On the fear itself Ellicott holds that the original leaves no doubt the readers had been tempted, the only doubt being how they had borne it, and that the word for the tempter marks not merely his character but his constant occupation. Calvin says the same of the office and adds that the writer now states plainly what he had at first avoided as too harsh, his fear that the labour had been wasted. Robertson reports one scholar taking the clause as a question expecting the answer no, and prefers to read it as a fear about something already past. Barnes makes Satan the real author of the persecution, the Jews being the immediate actors under his direction. Gill notes that the writer has slipped into the singular here, which he thinks throws light back on the plural used earlier.
6:
The verb used of Timothy's report is the one ordinarily rendered "preached the gospel," and Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson all pause on it, since here the good news is about a congregation rather than from God. Gill draws a conclusion from the meeting place that contradicts the letter's own subscription: Timothy came to Corinth, not Athens, so the letter was written from there. Clarke reconstructs the whole itinerary to the same end, having the two companions left behind when the persecution drove the writer out, summoned to Athens, one of them sent back again, and the meeting finally taking place at Corinth. Robertson admits one loose thread, that it is not clear why Silas goes unnamed here. The report itself Clarke numbers in three: they stood fast in the faith, they loved one another, and they remained attached to the apostle. Ellicott distinguishes the first two as the confidence in God that enabled them to endure and the tenderness with which they carried each other through, and reads the remembrance as kind rather than merely vivid, since a congregation beginning to fall away would not have wished to see its teachers again. Calvin says the two words together contain the whole sum of true piety.

Barnes notes that the affection ran both ways, there being no sign that they blamed him for leaving or for staying away, and Henry makes the mutuality the lesson, that no love was lost on either side and that it is a happy thing when minister and people love each other so, the world hating both. On the declaration that follows, Gill takes the writer to have been until then a dead man, lifeless and dispirited, carrying about the dying of the Lord Jesus, and revived by the news as by life from the dead. Calvin puts it as a sentence the writer might have spoken: though in myself I am dead, yet in your welfare I live; and turns it into a standard for pastors, who should count themselves happy when the church prospers though they are otherwise encompassed with miseries, and pine with grief when the building decays though all else goes well. Barnes reaches for a Latin epigram to the effect that life consists not in living but in health. Ellicott hears the conditional clause as half future, the continuance of that life hanging on their steadfastness, and reports a rival reading which makes both pronouns general, dismissing it as suiting neither the Greek nor the context.

Ellicott reads the question about thanks as an apology for the three extravagant verses before it, and locates the occasion in prayer. Calvin says the writer asks himself the question because he can find no expression of gratitude equal to the joy, and Gill that he knew neither where to begin nor when to end. On the adverb piled up in the next verse Robertson supplies the picture, one word meaning abundantly, a second out of bounds, and this third more than out of bounds, so that all bounds overflow; Clarke renders it abounding and superabounding in entreaty. The verb for what was wanting is a mending word, used of nets and of men, and Barnes lists the range it covers elsewhere, fitting, restoring, framing and joining together. Calvin draws the sharpest lesson from it: we may never congratulate men in this life so unqualifiedly as to stop desiring something better for them, since they are still on the road and may fall back, and those who far surpass others remain far from the goal. Ellicott notes the unflattering honesty of a teacher who tells converts their faith is deficient, and adds a reason for the vehemence of the praying, that the obstacle was believed to be the adversary's and not God's will, which is why it could be prayed against at all.
11:
The prayer names two subjects and takes a singular verb, and four of the commentators stop on that fact independently. Robertson records it plainly, noting also that one article covers the first pair of titles while a second stands before the name of Jesus, and that a third-person optative of wish is elsewhere almost unknown in the New Testament. Ellicott reports that some divines argue from the singular for the substantial unity of the Son with the Father, cautions that it must not be pressed so hard as to imply a unity of person, and still grants that the wish assumes the equality of the two and that the plural would have been unthinkable. Henry draws the conclusion without hedging: prayer is religious worship and worship is due to God alone, so a prayer addressed to Christ makes Christ God as the Father is God. Barnes puts it as a question, asking whether the writer would have prayed to an angel to direct his way. Calvin reaches it from the office rather than the grammar, that the same work is assigned to both because the Father confers no blessing except through the hand of the Son.

Who is meant by "the Lord" in the next verse divides them three ways. Barnes and Robertson take it for Jesus, that being the name commonly so used, and read the verse as a petition addressed to him. Ellicott doubts the restriction, thinking the word here stands for the name of God generally rather than for the Son alone. Gill takes it for the Spirit, and says so in order to make the point that the persons addressed across these two verses are Father, Son and Spirit together, the Spirit being God equally with them and therefore a fit object of prayer, which otherwise he would not be. On the two verbs of increase Robertson admits he can see little difference between them; Ellicott finds a sequence, the first meaning multiplication and the second the state of having enough and to spare, with the widening from one another to all men marking the same advance. Calvin has the love begin with the household of faith and go out to the whole human race, the nearer connection cherished without the more distant being crowded out, and insists that the increase of love is God's work no less than its beginning, which he takes to settle how far the commandments measure our strength.

Ellicott calls the link between the two clauses beautiful, settled holiness being the object and overflowing love toward mankind the means to it. Gill takes hearts to be named because they are the unstable thing, inconstant in their frames and needing to be fixed against the fears of men and the frowns of the world. Calvin reads the word as the innermost part of the soul, so that a man is acceptable only when his holiness is internal and not merely external; he then raises the objection himself, that if we stand at the judgment seat by holiness there is nothing left for the pardon of sins to do, and answers that pardon is not excluded but presupposed, faith coming first as a foundation comes before a building. Clarke makes love the thing that produces both solidity and continuance, so that a man filled with it is unblameable because love is the fulfilling of the law. On the company named at the end the two who address it differ: Barnes includes both the attending angels and the whole number of the redeemed, while Ellicott, though allowing that the word could be stretched to cover angels, thinks the writer is anticipating what he says a chapter later, and reads the Greek as hinting that these are to sit as assessors in the judgment.
